tasks.title: Where am I?
tasks.text: Welcome aboard, dockhand. Every terminal session starts inside some folder. Ask the computer which one with `pwd` (print working directory).
tasks.goal: Print your current folder.
tasks.after: /home/cadet is your home folder. The ~ in your prompt is shorthand for it.

tasks.title: Look around
tasks.text: Let’s see what’s in your home folder. `ls` lists everything here.
tasks.goal: List the files in this folder.
tasks.after: Blue names are folders. White names are files.

tasks.title: Read the welcome note
tasks.text: There’s a note waiting for you. `cat` prints a file’s contents to the screen.
tasks.goal: Read welcome.txt.
tasks.hint: `cat welcome.txt` (try typing cat wel and pressing Tab).
tasks.after: cat is short for “concatenate”, because it can join several files into one output.

tasks.title: Hidden things
tasks.text: Rumor says the captain hid something here. Files that start with a dot are hidden from a plain `ls`. The `-a` flag shows all of them.
tasks.goal: Find the hidden file and read it.
tasks.after: Try ls -l as well: it shows permissions, sizes and dates for each file.

tasks.title: Change rooms
tasks.text: The harbor website lives in projects/webapp. Move into that folder with `cd` (change directory).
tasks.goal: Go into the projects/webapp folder.
tasks.after: Paths without a leading / start from where you are now. Paths that start with / start from the very top.

tasks.title: Home sweet home
tasks.text: `..` means “the folder above this one”, and `~` always means home.
tasks.goal: Get back to your home folder.
learn: Go up one folder / go home
tasks.after: Plain cd with nothing after it also takes you home.

tasks.title: Make a folder
tasks.text: The captain wants backups kept tidy. Create a new folder with `mkdir` (make directory).
tasks.goal: Create a folder called backups in your home folder.
tasks.after: Folders are just containers for files. You can nest them as deep as you like.

tasks.title: Write a file
tasks.text: `echo` prints text. Add `>` and a file name, and the text goes into that file instead of the screen.
tasks.goal: Create todo.txt in your home folder with some text inside.
tasks.hint: `echo "check the cargo" > todo.txt`, then `cat todo.txt` to see it.
tasks.after: Careful: > replaces whatever was in the file before.

tasks.title: Add a line
tasks.text: Using `>` again would wipe todo.txt. Two arrows, `>>`, add to the end instead.
tasks.goal: Add a second line to todo.txt without losing the first.
learn: Add a line to the end of a file
tasks.after: Logs grow exactly like this: programs keep appending new lines to the end.

tasks.title: Make a copy
tasks.text: Copy the shipment schedule into your backups folder with `cp SOURCE DESTINATION`.
tasks.goal: Copy notes.txt into backups.
tasks.after: Ending the destination with / makes it clear you mean “into this folder”.

tasks.title: Rename it
tasks.text: There’s no rename command in Linux. You “move” a file to a new name with `mv`.
tasks.goal: Rename todo.txt to tasks.txt.
tasks.after: mv into a folder moves the file there, like: mv tasks.txt backups/

tasks.title: Clear the clutter
tasks.text: An old log in /tmp is wasting space. Delete it with `rm`. The path starts with `/`, so it works from any folder.
tasks.goal: Delete /tmp/old-cargo.log.
tasks.after: rm deletes straight away. There’s no trash can in the terminal, so double-check before you press Enter.

tasks.title: Folders inside folders
tasks.text: Plain `mkdir` fails if the parent folders don’t exist yet. One extra flag creates the whole chain at once.
tasks.goal: Create archive/2026/november in your home folder, in one command.
tasks.after: -p also stays quiet if the folder already exists, which makes it handy in scripts.

tasks.title: Copy a whole folder
tasks.text: `cp` refuses to copy a folder unless you tell it to go recursive, which means copying everything inside too.
tasks.goal: Copy the backups folder into archive/2026/november.
learn: Copy a folder and everything in it
tasks.after: Use tree archive to see the whole structure you just built.

tasks.title: Just the top
tasks.text: Log files can be huge. `head` shows only the first lines. Add `-n` and a number to choose how many.
tasks.goal: Show only the first 3 lines of logs/system.log.
tasks.after: Without -n, head shows 10 lines.

tasks.title: The latest news
tasks.text: New log lines get added at the bottom, so the end is where the latest news is. `tail` is head’s twin.
tasks.goal: Show the last 2 lines of logs/system.log.
tasks.after: On real servers, tail -f follows a log live as new lines arrive.

tasks.title: Find the errors
tasks.text: Something went wrong this morning. `grep` searches a file and shows only the lines that match.
tasks.goal: Show every line containing ERROR in logs/system.log.
tasks.after: grep is case-sensitive by default: ERROR and error are different to it.

tasks.title: Count them
tasks.text: The pipe `|` sends one command’s output into the next. `wc -l` counts lines. Put them together.
tasks.goal: Count the ERROR lines using a pipe.
learn: Send output of A into B
tasks.after: Four errors. Chaining small tools with | is the heart of Linux.

tasks.title: Case doesn’t matter
tasks.text: The harbor master wants every mention of seagulls, but people type it as Seagull, seagull, SEAGULL… Search for the lowercase word `seagull` and make grep ignore case.
tasks.goal: Find every line mentioning seagulls, in any capitalization.
tasks.after: Two seagull incidents. The sandwich one is still under investigation.

tasks.title: Which line?
tasks.text: To fix a problem you often need to know exactly where it is. grep can print line numbers with each match.
tasks.goal: Find which line of logs/system.log mentions Gate B.
tasks.hint: `grep -n "Gate B" logs/system.log` (quotes keep the two words together)
tasks.after: Quotes matter: without them, the shell would treat Gate and B as two separate words.

tasks.title: Lost and found
tasks.text: Somewhere under your projects folder is an old file called crate-manifest.txt. Nobody remembers where. `find` searches through folders for you.
tasks.goal: Find where crate-manifest.txt is hiding.
tasks.after: Now that you know the path, cat it. Crate 0003 looks interesting.

tasks.title: Every log file
tasks.text: `*` is a wildcard that matches anything. Combine it with find to list all files ending in .log under your home folder. Put the pattern in quotes so find gets it as-is.
tasks.goal: List every .log file under your home folder.
tasks.after: Wildcards also work directly in the shell: ls logs/*.log

tasks.title: Line up the crew
tasks.text: crew.txt is a mess. `sort` puts lines in alphabetical order.
tasks.goal: Show crew.txt sorted alphabetically.
tasks.after: sort -r reverses the order, and sort -n sorts numbers properly (so 10 comes after 9).

tasks.title: No duplicates
tasks.text: Some crew members signed up twice. `uniq` removes repeated lines, but only when they’re next to each other. So sort first, then pipe into uniq.
tasks.goal: Show each crew member exactly once.
tasks.after: uniq -c also counts how many times each line appeared. You’ll need that later.

tasks.title: Read the fine print
tasks.text: Every file has permissions: who can read (r), write (w) and execute (x) it. A long listing shows them in the first column.
tasks.goal: Show a long listing of projects/webapp.
tasks.after: rw-r--r-- reads as three groups: you can read+write, your group can read, everyone else can read.

tasks.title: Permission to launch
tasks.text: In projects/webapp, try running the deploy script with `./deploy.sh`. It will refuse, because it lacks the x (execute) permission. `chmod +x` adds it.
tasks.goal: Make deploy.sh executable and run it.
tasks.after: The ./ means “the file right here”. Linux doesn’t run files from the current folder unless you say so.

tasks.title: Top secret
tasks.text: notes.txt holds shipment details. Right now anyone on the server can read it. Permissions can also be written as three digits: 4 = read, 2 = write, 1 = execute, added up for you, your group and everyone else.
tasks.goal: Make ~/notes.txt readable and writable by you only (rw-------).
tasks.hint: `chmod 600 ~/notes.txt` (6 = 4+2 for you, 0 for group, 0 for others)
learn: Only you can read and write
tasks.after: SSH keys must be 600, or ssh refuses to use them. Now you know why.

tasks.title: Write your own script
tasks.text: A script is just a text file full of commands. Create hello.sh in your home folder containing an echo that prints Ahoy, make it executable, and run it.
tasks.goal: Create and run a script that prints Ahoy.
tasks.after: Real scripts usually start with #!/bin/bash on the first line, telling the system which program runs them.

tasks.title: Remember this
tasks.text: Variables store values for later. Set one with `NAME=value` (no spaces around =), and read it back with `$NAME`.
tasks.goal: Store your name in a variable called CREW, then print it with echo.
tasks.after: Try echo $HOME and echo $USER too. Docker uses variables like these to configure containers.

tasks.title: Pack it up
tasks.text: A tar archive bundles many files into one, and the z flag compresses it. The flags read as: c create, z gzip, f file name next.
tasks.goal: Pack the backups folder into backups.tar.gz in your home folder.
tasks.after: Archives are how you back up, download and ship bundles of files.

tasks.title: Peek inside
tasks.text: You can list what’s in an archive without unpacking it. Swap c (create) for t (list).
tasks.goal: List the contents of backups.tar.gz.
tasks.after: Always peek before you unpack something someone sent you.

tasks.title: Unpack somewhere else
tasks.text: x extracts. Normally files land in the current folder, but -C picks a different destination.
tasks.goal: Extract backups.tar.gz into /tmp.
tasks.after: Memory trick: eXtract Ze Files, Create Ze File, Tell me what’s in Ze File.

tasks.title: Who’s running?
tasks.text: Every running program is a process with a number, its PID. `ps` lists your processes. `ps aux` lists everyone’s.
tasks.goal: List the running processes.
tasks.after: PID 1 is always the very first process, started when the machine boots.

tasks.title: The CPU hog
tasks.text: The server feels sluggish. `top` lists processes sorted by how much CPU they use.
tasks.goal: Find out which process is eating the CPU.
learn: See which processes use the most CPU
tasks.after: crane-sim is stuck in a loop at 99% CPU. Note its PID.

tasks.title: Stop the loop
tasks.text: `kill` followed by a PID asks a process to stop.
tasks.goal: Stop crane-sim.
tasks.hint: `kill 4242` (the PID you saw in top or ps)
tasks.after: Run top again: the load is back to normal.

tasks.title: The stubborn one
tasks.text: BWAAAMP. A fog-horn process just started and it won’t stop blaring. A plain kill politely asks a process to quit, and this one ignores polite requests.
tasks.goal: Force fog-horn to stop.
tasks.hint: Find its PID with `ps`, then `kill -9 PID` (9 is SIGKILL, which can’t be ignored)
tasks.alert: 📯 BWAAAMP. Something called fog-horn just started on the server.
tasks.after: Use -9 as a last resort: the process gets no chance to save its work or clean up.

tasks.title: Disk check
tasks.text: A full disk breaks almost everything. `df` shows how full each disk is, and `-h` makes the numbers human-readable (G for gigabytes).
tasks.goal: Check how full the disks are.
tasks.after: Use% is the number to watch. Anything over 90% needs attention.

tasks.title: What takes space?
tasks.text: df tells you a disk is full. `du` tells you what’s filling it. `-s` gives one total, `-h` makes it readable.
tasks.goal: Check how much space your home folder uses.
learn: Show how much space a folder uses
tasks.after: du -sh * shows the size of every item in the current folder, which is great for hunting down space hogs.

tasks.title: Your first container
tasks.text: Time for Docker. A container is like a shipping container for software: an app plus everything it needs, packed in one box that runs the same anywhere. Run the classic test image.
tasks.goal: Run the hello-world container.
tasks.after: Docker didn’t have the image yet, so it downloaded (pulled) it from Docker Hub first, then ran it.

tasks.title: Stock the yard
tasks.text: Images are the packed recipes that containers start from. Download the nginx web server image ahead of time.
tasks.goal: Pull the nginx image.
tasks.after: An image is the recipe. A container is one running copy of it. You can run many containers from one image.

tasks.title: Check the inventory
tasks.text: See which images are stored on this machine.
tasks.goal: List your images.
tasks.after: The IMAGE ID identifies an image even if it has several names.

tasks.title: Run it in the background
tasks.text: Start nginx as a background web server. `-d` runs it detached, `--name` names it, and `-p 8080:80` connects port 8080 on your machine to port 80 inside the container.
tasks.goal: Run nginx in the background, named web, on port 8080.
tasks.after: Your web server is up and running.

tasks.title: What’s running?
tasks.text: List the containers that are running right now.
tasks.goal: Show running containers.
tasks.after: Look at the PORTS column: 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp is the mapping you asked for.

tasks.title: Pay a visit
tasks.text: Your web server is published on port 8080. `curl` fetches a web page right in the terminal.
tasks.goal: Fetch the page served on port 8080.
learn: Fetch a web page from the terminal
tasks.after: localhost means “this machine”. The request went to port 8080, and Docker forwarded it to port 80 inside the container.

tasks.title: Read the logs
tasks.text: When a container misbehaves, its logs are the first place to look.
tasks.goal: Show the logs of the web container.
tasks.after: See the GET line at the bottom? That’s your curl visit.

tasks.title: Step inside
tasks.text: `docker exec` runs a command inside a running container. Peek at the files nginx serves from /usr/share/nginx/html.
tasks.goal: List /usr/share/nginx/html inside web.
learn: Run a command inside a container
tasks.after: On a real machine, docker exec -it web sh opens a full shell inside the container.

tasks.title: Unload the ship
tasks.text: Done with nginx. A container must be stopped before it can be removed.
tasks.goal: Stop and remove the web container.
tasks.hint: `docker stop web` then `docker rm web` (or both at once: `docker stop web && docker rm web`)
tasks.after: docker rm -f web stops and removes in one step.

tasks.title: Build your own
tasks.text: The webapp folder has a Dockerfile: step-by-step instructions for packing the app into an image. Read it, then build it. The `.` means “use this folder”.
tasks.goal: Build an image called myapp from ~/projects/webapp.
learn: Build an image from a Dockerfile
tasks.after: Each line of a Dockerfile is a step. Docker caches the steps, so rebuilds are fast when little has changed.

tasks.title: Launch day
tasks.text: Your app listens on port 5000 inside the container. Run your very own image in the background and publish that port.
tasks.goal: Run myapp in the background on port 5000, then visit it.
tasks.after: You built and shipped your own app. Try curl localhost:5000 if you haven’t yet.

tasks.title: The full picture
tasks.text: Containers that finished or crashed don’t vanish. They stay around, stopped, until you remove them.
tasks.goal: List every container, including stopped ones.
tasks.after: The hello-world container from earlier is still there, stopped.

tasks.title: Sweep the deck
tasks.text: That old hello-world container is just taking up space. Remove it, using the name or ID from the list.
tasks.goal: Remove the stopped hello-world container.
tasks.hint: `docker ps -a` to find its name, then `docker rm NAME` (or `docker container prune -f` removes every stopped container)
tasks.after: Docker gives unnamed containers random names like jolly_otter. Naming them yourself with --name keeps things tidy.

tasks.title: Clear the shelf
tasks.text: You won’t need the hello-world image again either. Removing an image uses a different command from removing a container.
tasks.goal: Delete the hello-world image.
tasks.after: Docker refuses to delete an image while any container (even a stopped one) still uses it.

tasks.title: A database appears
tasks.text: The harbor needs a database. Start a postgres container in the background, named db.
tasks.goal: Start postgres in the background with the name db.
tasks.after: Docker printed an ID, so it started… but is it still running? Check docker ps.

tasks.title: Why did it stop?
tasks.text: db isn’t in docker ps anymore. A container that stops right away almost always explains why in its logs.
tasks.goal: Read db’s logs to find out why it stopped.
tasks.after: Postgres refuses to start without a password, passed in as an environment variable.

tasks.title: Fix the database
tasks.text: Environment variables configure containers. Pass one with `-e NAME=value`. You can’t change a container’s settings after it’s created, so remove the broken db and start a new one.
tasks.goal: Get a postgres container named db running, with a password.
tasks.hint: `docker rm db` then `docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres`
tasks.after: Run docker logs db again: “ready to accept connections”.

tasks.title: Where’s the database?
tasks.text: Every container gets its own IP address. `docker inspect` shows everything Docker knows about a container as JSON, including that.
tasks.goal: Find db’s IP address.
tasks.hint: `docker inspect db` and look for IPAddress, or the short way: `docker inspect -f "{{.NetworkSettings.IPAddress}}" db`
learn: See every detail of a container
tasks.after: IPs can change when containers restart, which is why you’ll connect containers by name instead in a moment.

tasks.title: Safe storage
tasks.text: Containers are disposable: remove one and every file inside it is gone. Volumes store data outside the container, so it survives.
tasks.goal: Create a volume called harbor-data.
tasks.hint: `docker volume create harbor-data`, then `docker volume ls` to check
tasks.after: Databases and anything else that saves data should always use a volume.

tasks.title: Mount the volume
tasks.text: `-v VOLUME:/path` plugs a volume into a container at a folder. Redis saves its data in /data.
tasks.goal: Run redis in the background, named cache, with harbor-data mounted at /data.
tasks.after: Now you could delete cache and start a new one with the same volume, and the data would still be there. Try docker exec cache redis-cli ping too.

tasks.title: A private network
tasks.text: On Docker’s default network, containers can’t find each other by name. Your own network fixes that.
tasks.goal: Create a network called harbor-net.
tasks.hint: `docker network create harbor-net`, then `docker network ls`
tasks.after: Containers on the same user-made network can reach each other by container name, with no IPs needed.

tasks.title: Plug it in
tasks.text: cache is already running. You can connect a running container to another network without restarting it.
tasks.goal: Connect cache to harbor-net.
learn: Add a container to a network
tasks.after: cache is now on two networks: the default bridge and harbor-net.

tasks.title: Can you hear me?
tasks.text: Prove the network works. Start a throwaway alpine container on harbor-net that pings cache once. `--rm` removes it automatically when it’s done.
tasks.goal: Ping cache by name from a temporary container on harbor-net.
tasks.after: Try the same without --network harbor-net and you’ll get “bad address”. That’s why custom networks matter.

tasks.title: One file to rule them all
tasks.text: Starting containers one by one gets tedious. Docker Compose describes a whole stack in a single YAML file. Go to ~/projects/stack and read docker-compose.yml.
tasks.goal: Read the stack’s docker-compose.yml.
learn: Describe a whole stack in one file
tasks.after: Two services: web (nginx) and cache (redis), with a volume for the cache. depends_on makes cache start first.

tasks.title: Raise the stack
tasks.text: One command creates the network, the volume and every container in the file. Remember the flag that keeps things running in the background.
tasks.goal: Start the whole stack in the background.
tasks.after: Compose named everything after the folder: stack-web-1, stack-cache-1, stack_default. Try curl localhost:8081.

tasks.title: Stack status
tasks.text: docker ps shows every container on the machine. Compose has its own version that shows only this stack.
tasks.goal: List only this stack’s containers.
tasks.after: docker compose logs shows all services’ output together, labeled by service.

tasks.title: Strike the stack
tasks.text: When you’re done, Compose can tear everything down as easily as it built it.
tasks.goal: Stop and remove the stack’s containers and network in one command.
tasks.after: The volume survives a down on purpose, so your data is safe. down -v deletes volumes too.

tasks.title: Challenge: squatter
tasks.text: 📟 Incident: the harbor site must go live on host port 8080, as a container named harbor running your myapp image (which listens on 5000 inside). Something is already sitting on that port. You’re on your own now.
tasks.goal: Get harbor running myapp on host port 8080.
tasks.hint: `docker ps` shows squatter on 8080. `docker rm -f squatter`, then `docker run -d --name harbor -p 8080:5000 myapp`
tasks.alert: 📟 Pager: “Port 8080 is serving the wrong site. Find out what’s on it.”
learn: Find and free a busy port
tasks.after: Two containers can never publish the same host port at once. docker ps is always the first place to look.

tasks.title: Challenge: broken build
tasks.text: Build an image called fixed from ~/projects/broken. The build fails. Read the error carefully, fix the Dockerfile, and build again. There’s no text editor here, so you’ll need a command that edits files in place.
tasks.goal: Build the fixed image successfully.
tasks.hint: The error points at line 2: FORM should be FROM. `cd ~/projects/broken`, `sed -i 's/FORM/FROM/' Dockerfile`, `docker build -t fixed .`
tasks.after: Build errors always say which line broke. Reading the error closely solves most problems.

tasks.title: Challenge: disk full
tasks.text: 📟 The server’s disk is almost full and services are starting to fail. Find what’s eating the space under /var/log and get rid of it.
tasks.goal: Free up the disk.
tasks.hint: `df -h` confirms it, `du -sh /var/log/*` finds the culprit, `rm /var/log/crane-debug.log` fixes it
learn: Track down what fills a disk
tasks.after: Somebody left debug logging switched on. On real servers, log rotation stops this from happening.

tasks.title: Challenge: log detective
tasks.text: Which log level (INFO, WARN or ERROR) appears most often in logs/system.log? Answer it with one pipeline that counts every level, most common first. Hint: the level is the third word on each line.
tasks.goal: Count each log level in a single pipeline.
tasks.hint: `awk '{print $3}' logs/system.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` (from your home folder)
tasks.after: This exact pipeline is how people find the most common errors, IPs or URLs in real logs.

tasks.title: Final mission: ship 1.0
tasks.text: Time to ship a proper release. Give myapp a version tag of 1.0, then run exactly that version in the background as app-prod, on harbor-net, reachable on host port 9000.
tasks.goal: Run myapp:1.0 as app-prod on harbor-net, on port 9000.
tasks.hint: `docker tag myapp myapp:1.0`, then `docker run -d --name app-prod --network harbor-net -p 9000:5000 myapp:1.0`
tasks.after: Tagged, networked, published. That’s a real deployment.
